study_design: One-to-one age- and race-matched hospital-based case-control study.
cohort_total_n_excerpt: This is a one-to-one, age- and race-matched case-control study involving 55 histologically confirmed black prostate cancer patients and 55 controls who were seen at three major hospitals in Washington, DC from 1982 to 1984.
reason: The study compares nutrient intake between prostate cancer cases and controls. No aggressive prostate cancer subtype or endpoint is analyzed.

estimate_classifications.endpoint_excerpt: There was a significant negative association between linoleic acid (p less than 0.04) for the 50 years and older group, thiamin (p less than 0.05) for those 30-49 years old, riboflavin (p less than 0.03) for the 50 and older group, and iron (p less than 0.05) for those 30-49 years old.
estimate_classifications.reason: The iron comparison is between overall prostate cancer cases and controls, with no aggressive disease definition.

estimate_classifications.endpoint_excerpt: There was a significant negative association between linoleic acid (p less than 0.04) for the 50 years and older group, thiamin (p less than 0.05) for those 30-49 years old, riboflavin (p less than 0.03) for the 50 and older group, and iron (p less than 0.05) for those 30-49 years old.
estimate_classifications.reason: Thiamin, or vitamin B1, is evaluated in overall prostate cancer cases and controls rather than an aggressive subtype.

estimate_classifications.endpoint_excerpt: The results of this study suggest that the intake of thiamin and iron (in subjects 30-49 years old), linoleic acid and riboflavin (in subjects 50 years and over) could be protective because control subjects consumed more of these nutrients than did the cases.
estimate_classifications.reason: The thiamin comparison concerns overall prostate cancer case status and does not distinguish aggressive disease.
